strengths: Resolves an explicit open question from Balcan et al. (2025): the paper provides the first general sample-complexity (pseudo-dimension) guarantees for tuning multi-dimensional hyperparameters (α ∈ R^p, p > 1) in the bi-level (f ≠ g) data-driven setting, where prior work was restricted to one-dimensional α and f ≡ g.

The core technical contribution, Theorem 4.1, is a clean and reusable 'engine' connecting logical definability to statistical learnability: pseudo-dimension is bounded via quantifier-elimination complexity of polynomial first-order formulas. The claimed refinement over Goldberg & Jerrum (1993) — removing dependence on the data dimension q and a factor p in log M — is meaningful and well-motivated.

The logic-based approach eliminates the need for the strong boundary regularity assumptions (e.g., ELICQ) required by the geometric analysis of Balcan et al. (2025), which is a genuine methodological advantage, and the framework extends beyond piecewise polynomial to general semi-algebraic functions (Appendix C).

The paper demonstrates both generality and tightness: Section 7 / Appendix F.2 shows the refined bound (Theorem 7.2) recovers the matching Ω(d) lower bound for ElasticNet tuning from Balcan et al. (2023), and Section 8 gives new learnability results for weighted group LASSO (going beyond the piecewise polynomial assumption via a clever auxiliary-variable encoding) and weighted fused LASSO (via the mp-QP dual, Proposition G.1).

The bi-level validation-loss result (Theorem 6.1) is conceptually important: it removes the unrealistic restriction that training and validation objectives coincide, which prior work required, and the proof construction (encoding the optimality predicate ∃θ' with f(α,θ') < f(α,θ)) is correct and transparent.

Honest limitations discussion: the conclusion explicitly identifies the absence of minimax lower bounds for the general implicitly-defined bi-level setting and the restriction to semi-algebraic (polynomial) structures, with a plausible path forward via o-minimal structures.
weaknesses: The bounds are upper bounds only; no lower bounds are established for the general multi-dimensional bi-level setting (Theorem 6.1), so the tightness of the main results (e.g., the p²d² dependence) remains unverified except in the special solution-path case. The work is consequently more of a solid framework than a sharp characterization.

The contribution, while resolving a real open question, is methodologically incremental: it is a careful and well-executed application of known quantifier-elimination machinery (Basu-Pollack-Roy) combined with the GJ framework (Bartlett et al., 2022) to a setting whose difficulty was already well understood. The novelty lies in the observation and the refinement, not in new tools.

Non-trivial sloppiness in the appendices undermines confidence on close reading: e.g., in Appendix C the graph of x/y is incorrectly stated as {(x,y) | xy = 1}; the proof of Theorem 8.2 conflates Mpath (number of boundary functions) with Tpath (number of regions), writing 'Mpath ≤ 3^p' for the region count; Theorem 7.2's statement contains an undefined variable ('θ*(α, w)'); several cross-references are wrong ('Theorem 7.1' where Theorem 7.2 is meant, in Section 7 and Remark F.3); and there are typos in formulas (e.g., T2 in Appendix G.1 uses b instead of b'). None appear fatal, but they should be corrected.

The practical scope of the guarantees is limited: the complexity parameters (Mf, Tf, ∆f) for realistic problem classes can be exponential in the model dimension (e.g., Tpath = O(3^d) for ElasticNet), so the resulting sample complexities, while asymptotically informative, may be large; the paper does not discuss when these bounds are practically meaningful.

The empirical relevance of the training-loss setting (Section 5, f ≡ g) is questionable — tuning α to minimize training loss is rarely done in practice — so roughly a third of the technical development addresses a setting of limited applied interest, included mainly to enable direct comparison with Balcan et al. (2025).

No experiments or algorithmic illustrations are provided; this is acceptable for a theory paper, but even a small empirical demonstration of the learned hyperparameters (e.g., for weighted fused LASSO) would have strengthened the significance claim.

strengths: Resolves a genuine open question from Balcan et al. (2025): the paper provides the first general pseudo-dimension upper bounds for data-driven tuning of multi-dimensional (α ∈ R^p) hyperparameters with implicitly defined bi-level losses, and removes the restrictive ELICQ-style regularity assumptions required by the prior geometric approach.

Theorem 4.1 is a clean and reusable result connecting FOL definability of a function class to its pseudo-dimension via quantifier elimination (Basu-Pollack-Roy) plus the Goldberg-Jerrum framework; the refinement over Goldberg & Jerrum (1993) — removing dependence on the data dimension q and a factor of p — is a real, independently useful improvement.

Good coverage of practically relevant variants: the training-loss setting (Thm 5.1), the bi-level validation-loss setting (Thm 6.1), approximate inner optimization (Prop 6.2), and tighter bounds when an explicit piecewise-rational solution path exists (Thm 7.2), with the ElasticNet corollary recovering the matching lower bound of Balcan et al. (2023) and hence demonstrating tightness in a concrete case.

The lower bound (Thm 5.2) adapts the bit-extraction technique to an implicitly optimized loss via a non-trivial stabilization argument (grid penalty forcing minimizers to a lattice), which is a nice technical contribution.

New learnability results for weighted group lasso (going beyond the piecewise-polynomial assumption via auxiliary variables) and weighted fused lasso (via mp-QP duality) illustrate the framework's scope on well-motivated sparse-learning problems.

Proofs are complete and generally follow a verifiable chain (FOL construction → QE complexity → GJ → Pollard), and the conclusion honestly identifies open problems (bi-level lower bound, extension to o-minimal structures).
weaknesses: Degree-accounting concern in the lower bound (Thm 5.2): the grid-penalty term ∏_{m=1}^d ∏_{k=0}^{K-1}(θ_m − k)^2 has total degree ≈ 2Kd = Θ(Δf · d), so the construction appears to violate the stated hypothesis 'f(x, α, θ) is a degree at most Δf' if degree means total degree (only the per-variable degree is ≤ Δf). Since the upper bound (Thm 5.1) is parametrized by total degree, this weakens the claimed tightness and needs clarification.

Inconsistency between Theorem 6.1 and its proof: the theorem states M_tot = M_f + T_f + M_g + T_g + d, but Appendix E derives M_total ≤ 4d + (M_g + T_g) + (2M_f + T_f^2), which includes a T_f^2 term (pairwise piece comparisons) absent from the theorem statement. This is likely only a constant factor in the log, but the statements should be reconciled.

Moderate conceptual novelty: Theorem 4.1 is essentially a composition of known machinery (Basu-Pollack-Roy quantifier elimination with the Goldberg-Jerrum/Bartlett et al. framework), and the main theorems are applications of it; the contribution is an extension/generalization of Balcan et al. (2025) rather than a new technique.

The 'first general framework for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning' framing is somewhat overstated: Balcan et al. (2023) already provided tight guarantees for the two-dimensional elastic-net case, so the novelty is the general p-dimensional implicit framework, which should be stated more carefully.

The lower bound covers only the training-loss (f ≡ g) case; no lower bound is given for the bi-level validation setting, so the tightness of Theorem 6.1 (which carries p²d² factors and may be quite loose) remains unknown — acknowledged, but it limits the significance of the general upper bound.

Presentation is rough in places: typos ('Forth', 'cheking'), notation overloading (K as both quantifier count and grid size; Θ vs K^d), inconsistent symbols in Appendix G (b vs y, b̃/ỹ), and a proof of Theorem 5.2 with several unstated verifications (e.g., uniformity of the constant C and the Lipschitz constant L over the shattering set).

All bounds are worst-case algebraic-complexity bounds with no empirical component; this is acceptable for a theory paper, but the practical reach of the framework (e.g., whether the p², d² factors are meaningful) is untested.
